paragraphs: We have no well-documented records of Rome’s earliest period. Most of the stories told about it are very probably fables. In general, the most instructive part of any people’s history, the part about how it was founded, is the part we know least about. Experience shows us every day what causes lead to the revolutions of empires. But since no new peoples are formed now, we have almost nothing but guesswork to explain how they were created.

The customs we find established show at least that they had a beginning. The traditions that reach back to those beginnings, that rest on the greatest authorities and are backed by the strongest proofs, should count as the most certain. These are the rules I have tried to follow in asking how the freest and most powerful people on earth exercised its supreme power.

After Rome was founded, the new-born republic, meaning the army of its founder, made up of Albans, Sabines and foreigners, was divided into three groups. From this division they took the name _tribes_. Each tribe was split into ten _curiæ_, and each _curia_ into _decuriæ_, led by officers called _curiones_ and _decuriones_.

In addition, each tribe supplied a body of one hundred _Equites_, or Knights, called a _century_. This shows that these divisions, which a town had no need of, were at first purely military. Yet an instinct for greatness seems to have led the little town of Rome to give itself, in advance, a political system fit for the capital of the world.

This original division soon produced an awkward situation. The tribes of the Albans (Ramnenses) and the Sabines (Tatienses) always stayed the same size, while the tribe of the foreigners (Luceres) kept growing as more and more foreigners came to live in Rome, so that it soon outstripped the others in strength. Servius fixed this dangerous flaw by changing the basis of the division. He abolished the division by race and put in its place a new one, based on the quarter of the town each tribe lived in. Instead of three tribes he created four, each occupying one of the hills of Rome and named after it. In this way he corrected the inequality of the moment and also provided for the future. And so that the division would be one of persons as well as of places, he forbade the inhabitants of one quarter to move to another, which prevented the races from mixing.

He also doubled the three old centuries of Knights and added twelve more, keeping the old names. With this simple and prudent method he marked off the Knights from the people, and the people did not complain.

To the four urban tribes Servius added fifteen more, called rural tribes because they were made up of people living in the country, which was divided into fifteen cantons. Fifteen more were created later, and the Roman people ended up in thirty-five tribes, which is how it stayed until the end of the Republic.

The split between urban and rural tribes had one effect worth noting, both because nothing like it is found elsewhere and because Rome owed to it the preservation of her morals and the growth of her empire. We would expect the urban tribes to take over power and honors quickly and to start running down the rural tribes. What happened was exactly the opposite. The taste of the early Romans for country life is well known. They owed it to their wise founder, who tied farming and military service to liberty and, so to speak, banished arts, crafts, intrigue, fortune and slavery to the town.

Since all of Rome’s most illustrious citizens lived on the land and farmed it, people grew used to looking there, and nowhere else, for the mainstays of the republic. This was the way of life of the best patricians, so everyone honored it. The simple, hard-working life of the villager was preferred to the lazy, idle life of the _bourgeoisie_ of Rome. A man who would have been a wretched proletarian in town became a respected citizen as a farm laborer. Varro says, not without reason, that our great-souled ancestors set up the nursery of sturdy, brave men in the village: men who defended them in war and fed them in peace. Pliny states flatly that the country tribes were honored because of the men who made them up, while cowards whom people wanted to disgrace were moved to the town tribes as a public shame. The Sabine Appius Claudius, when he came to settle in Rome, was loaded with honors and enrolled in a rural tribe, which later took his family name. Finally, freedmen always entered the urban tribes and never the rural ones. Nor is there a single example in the whole Republic of a freedman, even once he had become a citizen, reaching any magistracy.
This was an excellent rule. But it was carried so far that it eventually brought a change in the political system, and certainly an abuse.

First, the censors had long claimed the right to transfer citizens arbitrarily from one tribe to another. They then allowed most people to enroll themselves in whatever tribe they liked. This permission certainly did no good, and it also took away one of the censorship’s greatest resources. Moreover, the great and powerful all had themselves enrolled in the country tribes, while the freedmen who had become citizens stayed with the common people in the town tribes. As a result, both kinds of tribe soon lost any local or territorial meaning. They became so mixed up that the members of one could not be told from those of another except by the registers. The idea of the word _tribe_ thus became personal instead of real, or rather came to be little more than a fantasy.
On top of this, the town tribes, being on the spot, were often the stronger in the comitia, and they sold the State to anyone who would stoop to buy the votes of the rabble that made them up.

The founder had set up ten _curiæ_ in each tribe, so the whole Roman people, which was then contained within the city walls, consisted of thirty _curiæ_. Each had its own temples, gods, officers, priests and festivals. The festivals were called _compitalia_ and matched the _paganalia_ that the rural tribes held in later times.

When Servius made his new division, the thirty _curiæ_ could not be shared equally among his four tribes, and he did not want to disturb them. So they became another way of dividing the inhabitants of Rome, entirely independent of the tribes. But the rural tribes and their members had nothing to do with _curiæ_: by then the tribes had become a purely civil institution, and since a new way of raising troops had been introduced, the military divisions of Romulus were no longer needed. So although every citizen was enrolled in a tribe, there were very many who did not belong to a _curia_.

Servius made yet a third division, quite separate from the two just described, and in its effects it became the most important of all. He distributed the whole Roman people into six classes, set apart neither by place nor by person but by wealth. The first classes held the rich, the last the poor, and those in between people of moderate means. These six classes were subdivided into one hundred and ninety-three other bodies, called centuries, and the division was made so that the first class alone had more than half of them, while the last had only one. So the class with the fewest members had the most centuries, and the whole last class counted as a single subdivision, although it alone held more than half the inhabitants of Rome.
